paragraphs.paragraph: All the inhabitants of the earth are called to make a joyful noise, sing, worship, and honor God's name, whose works are awesome and whose enemies submit before His power.
paragraphs.title: A Universal Call to Praise God

easy.explanation: Verse 1 calls all the lands to make a joyful noise unto God.
easy.q: Who is called to make a joyful noise unto God?

easy.explanation: Verse 2 says, “Sing forth the honour of his name.”
easy.q: What are they told to sing forth?

easy.explanation: Verse 3 asks, “How terrible art thou in thy works!”
easy.q: What does the psalmist call God's works?

medium.explanation: Verse 4 says, “All the earth shall worship thee, and shall sing unto thee.”
medium.q: What action is mentioned together with singing in verse 4?

answers: Raise a sound of joyful praise
medium.explanation: The phrase is a call to express joyful praise aloud.
medium.q: In this passage, what does “make a joyful noise” mean?

answers: Because of the greatness of His power
Because they are invited to judge Him
medium.explanation: Verse 3 connects their submission with the greatness of God's power.
medium.q: Why will God's enemies submit themselves unto Him?

answers: It is directed only to enemies
challenge.explanation: The expression extends the call to praise across all lands.
challenge.q: What does “all ye lands” show about the call to praise?

answers: His power causes them to submit
challenge.explanation: Verse 3 says that through the greatness of His power His enemies submit themselves unto Him.
challenge.q: What relationship is shown between God's power and His enemies?

answers: Joyful noise, singing, worship, and praise
challenge.explanation: The passage moves from a joyful cry to singing, worship, and honoring God's name.
challenge.q: Which sequence of worship appears in verses 1–4?

paragraphs.idea: All the inhabitants of the earth are called to make a joyful noise, sing, worship, and honor God's name, whose works are awesome and whose enemies submit before His power.

paragraphs.paragraph: The psalmist invites people to see God's works, recalls the sea becoming dry land and the crossing of the flood, describes God's rule over the nations, calls the people to bless Him, and thanks Him for preserving life.
paragraphs.title: God's Deeds and His Rule over the Nations

answers: Come and see the works of God
easy.explanation: Verse 5 says, “Come and see the works of God.”
easy.q: What does the psalmist invite people to do?

answers: He turned it into dry land
He covered the earth with it
easy.explanation: Verse 6 says, “He turned the sea into dry land.”
easy.q: What did God do to the sea?

easy.explanation: Verse 7 says, “He ruleth by his power for ever,” and mentions His eyes beholding the nations.
easy.q: Over whom does God rule by His power?

answers: Bless God and make His praise heard
medium.explanation: Verse 8 calls the people to bless God and make the voice of His praise heard.
medium.q: What should the people do after seeing God's works?

medium.explanation: “The rebellious” refers to people who resist or oppose authority.
medium.q: In verse 7, what does “the rebellious” describe?

answers: Describe the crossing as a failure
medium.explanation: After crossing on foot, the people say, “there did we rejoice in him.”
medium.q: What does the crossing of the sea and flood lead the people to do?

answers: He observes and rules over the nations
challenge.explanation: Verse 7 says, “his eyes behold the nations.”
challenge.q: What does God's watching the nations reveal?

answers: From seeing God's works to praising Him for His rule and preservation
From private prayer to offering sacrifices
challenge.explanation: The passage begins with seeing God's works, describes His rule, calls for praise, and ends with thanks for preserving life.
challenge.q: What movement of thought appears in verses 5–9?

answers: God preserves the lives of His people
challenge.explanation: Verse 9 praises God for keeping the soul alive and preventing the feet from being moved.
challenge.q: What does “holdeth our soul in life” mean?

paragraphs.idea: The psalmist invites people to see God's works, recalls the sea becoming dry land and the crossing of the flood, describes God's rule over the nations, calls the people to bless Him, and thanks Him for preserving life.

paragraphs.paragraph: God tested and refined His people through suffering, brought them into distress and under human rule, yet finally brought them through fire, water, and affliction into a wealthy place.
paragraphs.title: Trials, Refinement, and Deliverance into Relief

easy.explanation: Verse 10 says, “thou hast tried us, as silver is tried.”
easy.q: How did God prove His people?

easy.explanation: Verse 12 says, “we went through fire and through water.”
easy.q: Through what two elements did the people pass?

easy.explanation: The verse ends, “thou broughtest us out into a wealthy place.”
easy.q: Where did God finally bring them?

medium.explanation: Although they suffered affliction, God brought them out into a wealthy place.
medium.q: What came after the people's affliction and oppression?

medium.explanation: The comparison describes testing and refining through hardship.
medium.q: What does “as silver is tried” mean?

answers: Testing, affliction, fire and water, then deliverance
medium.explanation: The passage moves from testing and affliction through fire and water to deliverance.

answers: Suffering can serve as a process of testing and refining
The people were gathered to trade silver
challenge.explanation: The image of tried silver presents hardship as a testing and refining process.
challenge.q: What does the comparison with tried silver suggest?

answers: It emphasizes movement from danger and distress to deliverance and relief
It shows that fire and water are places of rest
It proves that the distress continued
challenge.explanation: The contrast highlights the change from severe hardship to a place of relief.
challenge.q: What is the effect of contrasting fire and water with a wealthy place?

answers: It describes submission under human oppression
It describes freedom from every burden
challenge.explanation: The image portrays the people as being subjected to human domination.
challenge.q: What does “thou hast caused men to ride over our heads” add to the description of suffering?

paragraphs.idea: God tested and refined His people through suffering, brought them into distress and under human rule, yet finally brought them through fire, water, and affliction into a wealthy place.

paragraphs.paragraph: After deliverance, the psalmist promises to enter God's house, fulfill his vows, and offer burnt offerings and sacrifices that he promised during his trouble.
paragraphs.title: Vows, Burnt Offerings, and Offerings of Thanks

answers: Into the house of his enemies
easy.explanation: Verse 13 says, “I will go into thy house with burnt offerings.”
easy.q: Where does the psalmist promise to go?

easy.explanation: He says, “I will pay thee my vows.”
easy.q: What does the psalmist promise to pay?

easy.explanation: Verses 13 and 15 mention burnt offerings and sacrifices.
easy.q: What does he plan to offer to God?

answers: After he had already received relief
medium.explanation: Verse 14 says his mouth spoke the vows “when I was in trouble.”
medium.q: When did the psalmist make his vows?

medium.explanation: The surrounding references to rams, bullocks, and goats show that these are sacrifices.
medium.q: What are “burnt offerings” in this passage?

answers: After deliverance, the psalmist fulfills what he vowed in trouble
He cancels his vows after deliverance
medium.explanation: The psalmist responds to deliverance by paying his vows and bringing offerings.
medium.q: What is the relationship between deliverance and the offerings?

answers: A change from prayer to warfare
challenge.explanation: Entering God's house with offerings shows thankful worship after distress.
challenge.q: What does the movement from trouble to God's house express?

answers: They identify the kinds of sacrifices to be offered
They describe animals in a fortress
They explain how the people crossed the river
challenge.explanation: The animals are listed as part of the offerings presented to God.
challenge.q: Why are rams, bullocks, and goats mentioned?

answers: Words spoken in trouble lead to a commitment to fulfill the vows
The lips are described as silent
The vows are shown to be unnecessary
challenge.explanation: The psalmist recalls what he said and promises to carry out those spoken vows.
challenge.q: What connection exists between “my lips have uttered” and “I will pay thee my vows”?

paragraphs.idea: After deliverance, the psalmist promises to enter God's house, fulfill his vows, and offer burnt offerings and sacrifices that he promised during his trouble.

paragraphs.paragraph: The psalmist invites those who fear God to hear what God has done for him, says that his prayer was heard because he did not regard iniquity in his heart, and ends by blessing God for His mercy.
paragraphs.title: Personal Testimony and an Answered Prayer

easy.explanation: Verse 16 addresses “all ye that fear God.”
easy.q: Whom does the psalmist invite to hear his testimony?

easy.explanation: Verse 17 says, “I cried unto him with my mouth.”
easy.q: What did the psalmist do with his mouth?

answers: He heard and attended to it
easy.explanation: Verse 19 says God heard him and attended to the voice of his prayer.
easy.q: What did God do to the psalmist's prayer?

answers: If he regarded iniquity in his heart
medium.explanation: The verse says, “If I regard iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear me.”
medium.q: Why would the Lord not hear the psalmist, according to verse 18?

medium.explanation: “Iniquity” refers to sin or wickedness regarded in the heart.
medium.q: What does “iniquity” mean in this context?

answers: By blessing God for hearing prayer and showing mercy
With a description of crossing a river
medium.explanation: Verse 20 blesses God for not turning away the prayer or His mercy.

answers: The psalmist makes his personal experience a testimony for others to hear
He hides his experience from everyone
He speaks only about his enemies
challenge.explanation: He invites those who fear God to hear what God has done for his soul.
challenge.q: How are personal testimony and the invitation to God's worshippers connected?

answers: Not regarding iniquity in the heart
challenge.explanation: The psalmist connects God's hearing with not cherishing iniquity in the heart.
challenge.q: What moral condition does the psalmist identify as important for prayer?

answers: The prayer is spoken, heard, and attended to
challenge.explanation: The passage moves from the psalmist crying out to God's hearing and attending to his prayer.
challenge.q: What does the repeated language of hearing show in verses 16–19?

paragraphs.idea: The psalmist invites those who fear God to hear what God has done for him, says that his prayer was heard because he did not regard iniquity in his heart, and ends by blessing God for His mercy.
